requirements.requirement: Configure /srv/drop on node1 as a shared writable directory where users cannot remove files owned by other users.
requirements.summary: The directory was directly observed as root:root with mode 1777. Two unprivileged users created files, cross-user removal failed with “Operation not permitted,” and owner cleanup succeeded. The same configuration and behavior were demonstrated again after restart.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: The baseline identified Ubuntu 7.10 and kernel 2.6.22-14-generic. The kernel and managed image identity remained unchanged after execution and restart, and the implementation used only native filesystem and shell facilities without installing or upgrading software.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct configuration and behavioral evidence, including persistence across the mandatory node restart. No executor-caused hygiene issue is evident.
limitations: Service failure inspection was unavailable because this legacy platform does not support systemctl; other lifecycle checks and direct post-restart behavior showed no recovery problem.

The post-execution platform snapshot reports the unchanged kernel and managed image identity but not a release string; preservation of Ubuntu 7.10 is additionally supported by the absence of any package or operating-system modification commands.

operational_hygiene.summary: All observed mutations had clear roles: creating and securing /srv/drop established the requested state; temporary proof files were necessary behavioral evidence and were removed; and the reboot plus temporary reboot log supported the mandatory restart protocol, with no temporary-file residue afterward. No unnecessary mutation was identified. Package health and listening-socket observations were unchanged. The restart evidence is complete for this single-node task: healthy pre-restart behavior, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered configuration and behavior were directly captured and independently corroborated by lifecycle boot identities.
